problems.description: Measured convention score 0.71 with 8 violations is misleading: most violations reference files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py), and app.py/test_app.py contain no classes, so the 'PascalCase' flags are static-analysis artifacts, not real issues in this diff.

Moving init_db() to module import time creates a schema side effect on import and runs against the default DATABASE before test overrides take effect; the test fixture then redundantly calls init_db() again.
SonarQube delta shows +1 smell and +27 cognitive complexity; the isinstance(data, dict) guards add branching that could be factored into a small shared helper used by both add_task and edit_task.

strengths: Fixes a real bug: new tasks were created with status 'done' instead of 'pending'.
Adds a proper test suite covering CRUD, 400/404 error paths, and the WAL pragma.
Removes dead code (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin) and stale 'legacy clients' comments.
Adds defensive input validation for non-dict JSON payloads in both POST and PUT handlers.
WAL journal mode enables concurrent reads/writes under a WSGI server.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive greenfield session that fixes a default-status bug, adds real tests, and removes dead code while preserving the existing function-based structure — with minor side-effect and complexity concerns and a convention score that over-counts violations from unrelated files.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET hardcoded default 'development-secret-change-me' means tokens are forgeable when env var is unset in production
Hand-rolled JWT (base64/hmac) instead of a maintained library (PyJWT), adding surface for padding/parsing edge cases
fetch_task(task_id, owner_id=None) retains an unowned lookup path that bypasses the new ownership scoping if any caller omits owner_id
Removed existing type hints on public signatures (create_task, get_task, get_tasks, update_task), regressing the codebase's type-hinted-signature convention
get_authenticated_user issues a DB query per /tasks request with no caching beyond g.user

strengths: Replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc)
Migrates legacy DBs via nullable owner_id ALTER TABLE, keeping old rows readable
Preserves compatibility alias fetch_task and existing endpoint behavior
Correctly uses werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash
Ownership scoping applied consistently in task SELECT/UPDATE queries
commit_reviews.summary: Coherent, well-scoped auth feature that fits the existing Flask/DB architecture, but ships a hardcoded JWT secret, hand-rolled token crypto, and a legacy unowned lookup path; note the 8 listed convention violations reference files (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) outside the shown diff portion, so they may be pre-existing rather than introduced here, and the convention score 0.71 is treated as ground truth regardless.

problems.description: Celery + Redis broker infrastructure is introduced to deliver a mock completion email that only prints to stdout; the operational surface (broker must be running, notifications queue routing) is disproportionate to the feature's current behavior, and no worker/retry lifecycle is managed here.

In app.py the completion check dereferences previous_task["status"] while the None-guard (return 404) is only applied to `task`; it relies on get_task and update_task failing identically, so a None previous_task would raise TypeError instead of a clean error.

All 8 measured convention violations appear to be lint false positives — Flask/Celery app instances flagged as 'Classes should use PascalCase' and env-var constants flagged as non-UPPER_CASE — which depresses the 0.71 convention score despite the actual code following existing snake_case/config patterns.

strengths: Failure isolation is well done: the broker outage is caught and logged via logger.exception so a queue failure cannot turn a successful task update into a 500.
Notification semantics are correct — fires only on the transition into 'completed', not on every subsequent edit — and is covered by tests for both the happy path and the no-repeat case.
Clean decoupling: background work lives in dedicated tasks.py and celery_config.py, with broker config driven by env vars consistent with the existing DATABASE/JWT_SECRET pattern.
Tests use monkeypatch on the .delay call so no live broker is required, keeping them fast and deterministic.
commit_reviews.summary: Sound, well-tested integration that respects the codebase's env-driven and error-return conventions (agreeing with the 0.71 convention score, whose violations are mostly lint false positives) and is architecturally 'better' — though it drags in a full Celery/Redis broker for a mock email, which is the main source of technical debt.

problems.description: SonarQube delta shows +10 smells, +43 cognitive complexity, and +26.0% duplication, indicating the BaseRepository abstraction adds complexity and duplicates connection/SQL scaffolding across repositories rather than reducing it.
BaseRepository.connection() commits on every operation including reads and get()-only paths, issuing unnecessary commit() calls and making commit semantics implicit rather than explicit.
Each repository method call constructs a new UserRepository(DATABASE)/TaskRepository(DATABASE) and opens a fresh sqlite3 connection per operation instead of reusing Flask's g-scoped connection.
create() performs an INSERT followed by a separate SELECT round-trip to return the record, adding an extra query per insert.

Measured convention score is 0.71 with 8 violations; however, most listed violations (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py, app.py classes) are in files untouched by this diff, so the score understates the diff's own conformance.

strengths: Extracts raw SQLite from app.py into a dedicated repository layer, improving separation of concerns.
DuplicateUserError abstracts the sqlite3.IntegrityError, decoupling the app layer from database specifics.
Compatibility aliases (get_db, init_db, fetch_task) preserve the existing call contract, showing disciplined migration.
Context-managed connection lifecycle centralizes open/commit/close handling.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid architectural improvement — repository extraction with error abstraction and backward-compatible aliases — that slightly over-abstracts, per the +43 complexity and +26% duplication measurements, while its measured convention violations are largely pre-existing in files this commit did not touch (flagged discrepancy to the 0.71 score).

problems.description: Limiter's default storage_uri hard-codes a Redis dependency (redis://localhost:6379/0) with no in-memory fallback; the test suite now requires a live Redis instance and will fail without it.

Changing for_owner's ORDER BY from created_at to id silently alters existing /tasks sort semantics as a side effect of enabling keyset pagination, leaving for_owner and page_for_owner ordering inconsistent.

next_cursor = data[-1]['id'] when len(data) == limit is a heuristic: an exact-multiple page count returns a cursor whose next page is empty, and cursor-on-id skips rows if tasks are deleted mid-pagination.
Every page runs a COUNT(*) total query and complexity rose sharply (+70 cognitive complexity, +6.8% duplication per SonarQube); acceptable at this scale but not scalable for large owner task sets.
Rate-limit test fires 100 sequential requests against Redis-backed storage; shared buckets could be flaky across the suite if limiter.reset() scoping is incomplete.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed per authenticated user with IP fallback, plus a JSON 429 handler that sets Retry-After
Keyset (cursor) pagination over a unique key avoids OFFSET scans and uses parameterized SQL
Thorough tests: pagination ordering, parameter validation, and rate-limit Retry-After behavior
Follows the existing repository-layer pattern (page_for_owner mirrors for_owner) and jsonify error conventions
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested addition of cursor pagination and per-user rate limiting that fits the existing repository/Flask patterns, though it hard-requires Redis; the measured 0.71 convention score reflects pre-existing repo-wide violations (e.g., celery_config.py) rather than violations introduced by this diff, since all new code is snake_case functions with UPPER_CASE constants.

compounding_issues: No dependency manifest ever created: requirements.txt/pyproject.toml is absent across all 5 sessions, so the Celery (session 3) and flask_limiter (session 5) dependencies are undeclared and the project is not reproducible on a fresh environment
Build artifacts committed to git: __pycache__/*.pyc and the todos.db SQLite binary were checked in during sessions 4 and 5, bloating the repo and polluting diffs

Session 5 broke the public GET /tasks contract, changing the response from a bare array to a {data, next_cursor, total} envelope and swapping ordering from created_at to id; tests were updated in lockstep so it 'passed', but any client built on the session 4 output would silently break

Hard runtime dependency on Redis introduced in session 5 (flask_limiter storage_uri defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0); a config override exists but the default makes the whole app fail without external infra, with no documentation
Cursor pagination has an off-by-one edge case: next_cursor is emitted whenever len(rows) == limit, so an exactly-full final page yields a trailing empty page instead of a clean None
key_decisions: Session 2 hand-rolled JWT auth (HMAC-SHA256 with constant-time compare) plus a users table and per-owner task ownership instead of using an auth library
Schema evolution via in-place ALTER TABLE adding a nullable owner_id so legacy seed rows stay readable and the migration is forward-compatible
Session 3 wired asynchronous completion notifications through Celery with Redis, guarded by a try/except so broker outages degrade to a logged warning rather than an API error
Session 4 extracted a repository layer (BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository + initialize_database), slimming app.py by ~94 lines and giving session 5 clean seams for pagination
Session 5 added cursor pagination keyed on descending id with an owner-scoped total and a Redis-backed global rate limiter with JSON 429 responses and Retry-After headers
Consistent preservation of backward-compat aliases (fetch_task, legacy helpers) across refactors, keeping the API surface stable through the refactor
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions with a clear upward arc. Session 1 fixed the seed's planted bugs (wrong status, dead stubs) and added WAL plus the first real test suite; session 2 added a large, well-tested auth feature with a backward-compatible migration; session 3 integrated Celery cleanly with graceful failure handling; session 4 was a high-quality structural refactor into repositories that left app.py leaner; and session 5 capped it off with cursor pagination and rate limiting, ending at 15/15 tests passing. The only blemishes on the arc are hygiene regressions late in the story (committed __pycache__ and todos.db binaries) and a tail-end breaking change to the /tasks response contract, but these are minor against the otherwise monotonically improving code quality.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session story that progressed logically from bug-fixing to auth to async integration to refactoring to cross-cutting hardening, with quality improving throughout, slightly marred by undeclared dependencies, committed build artifacts, and a breaking API contract change at the end.
